title: THE FEAR THAT MAKES YOU RUN FROM GOD… EVEN AFTER HE HAS FORGIVEN YOU
paragraphs: THE FEAR THAT MAKES YOU RUN FROM GOD… EVEN AFTER HE HAS FORGIVEN YOU

“Perfect Love Casts Out Fear” — But John Wasn't Talking About Every Fear. He Was Exposing the Terrifying Reason Some Christians Still Live Like Condemned Criminals After Jesus Has Already Paid Their Debt.
There is a kind of fear that doesn't make you scream.
It makes you pray with your head down.
It makes you worship while secretly wondering whether God is disappointed in you.
It makes you say, “God is good,” while a quieter voice inside your chest whispers, “But maybe not to someone like me.”
And sometimes, the most frightening place to experience that fear isn't inside a hospital room, a financial crisis, or a season of terrible uncertainty.
Sometimes it's in church.
Surrounded by people singing about grace.
While you're silently wondering whether that grace still includes you.
You know the Scriptures. You've heard the sermons. You believe Jesus died for sinners.
But there's something you haven't been able to shake.
The memory of what you did.
The person you hurt.
The promise you broke.
The temptation you returned to after swearing you never would.
And when someone tells you that perfect love casts out fear, you almost feel guilty for still being afraid.
Because if God's love is perfect, why does your heart still tremble?
Does that mean your faith is defective?
Does that mean you don't really know Jesus?
Does that mean something is terribly wrong with you?
Before you answer, you need to understand something John wrote nearly two thousand years ago.
Because one of the most comforting verses in the Bible has also become one of the most misunderstood.
And the truth hidden in its context may change the way you approach God for the rest of your life.
The apostle John wrote:
“There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love.” — 1 John 4:18 (KJV)
Beautiful words.
But read them carelessly, and you might conclude that every anxious thought, every nervous moment, every trembling prayer, and every experience of fear proves that God's love hasn't reached you.
That is not what John was saying.
And we know this because of what he wrote immediately before it.
“Herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment: because as he is, so are we in this world.” — 1 John 4:17 (KJV)
Did you catch it?
The day of judgment.
John wasn't primarily discussing your fear of tomorrow's bills.
He wasn't promising that genuine Christians would never feel afraid during illness, persecution, danger, or uncertainty.
He was speaking about something far more serious.
The fear of standing before the holy God as someone expecting condemnation.
The fear that the final verdict will be against you.
The fear that when everything hidden is revealed, your sins will speak louder than the Savior you claim to trust.
And John says that God's love, brought to its intended maturity in us, drives out that terror.
Not because sin suddenly becomes harmless.
Not because judgment is imaginary.
Not because God has lowered His standard of holiness.
But because Jesus Christ has done something for guilty people that guilty people could never accomplish for themselves.
And to understand how extraordinary that is, we need to look at John's original words.
The Greek text of 1 John 4:18 begins:
φόβος οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ
Phobos ouk estin en tē agapē.
Literally, “Fear is not in love.”
The word φόβος (phobos) means fear, dread, or alarm. By itself, it can describe different kinds of fear. But here, its meaning is shaped by John's surrounding discussion of judgment and punishment.
Then John writes:
ἀλλ’ ἡ τελεία ἀγάπη ἔξω βάλλει τὸν φόβον
All’ hē teleia agapē exō ballei ton phobon.
“But perfect love casts out fear.”
The word τελεία (teleia) comes from the Greek word family associated with completion, maturity, or reaching an intended goal.
John is not saying you must manufacture emotionally flawless love before God will accept you.
He is describing love reaching its intended fullness.
And notice the force of the expression ἔξω βάλλει (exō ballei).
It means “casts out” or “drives outside.”
John doesn't describe love politely negotiating with this fear.
He describes love expelling it.
Why?
Because he continues:
ὅτι ὁ φόβος κόλασιν ἔχει
Hoti ho phobos kolasin echei.
“Because fear has punishment.”
The Greek noun κόλασις (kolasis) refers to punishment. The King James Version renders it “torment,” emphasizing the distress associated with this fear.
John's argument is not merely that fear feels uncomfortable.
It is that this particular fear is connected to punishment.
The terrified conscience anticipates a sentence.
The guilty heart expects a verdict.
And the person who has not yet learned to rest in God's redeeming love may continue living beneath the shadow of condemnation.
That is the fear John is addressing.
And suddenly, his words become intensely personal.
Because there are people reading this right now who believe Jesus can forgive sinners in general…
But struggle to believe He has truly forgiven them.
They can celebrate someone else's testimony.
They can rejoice when a prodigal comes home.
They can quote Romans 8:1 to a struggling friend.
Yet when they remember their own past, they quietly wonder whether the promise has an exception.
An exception with their name on it.
Perhaps that person is you.
You have confessed the sin.
You have cried over it.
You have asked God for forgiveness more times than you can count.
Yet the memory keeps returning.
And every time it returns, you feel as though you must begin the entire process of earning God's acceptance again.
So you pray longer.
You serve harder.
You try to be better.
Not simply because you love Jesus, but because somewhere beneath your religious activity is a frightened thought:
Maybe if I do enough, God won't reject me.
That is a devastating way to live.
Not because prayer, obedience, service, and repentance are unimportant.
They are essential expressions of living faith.
But none of them can become the payment for a debt that only Christ could pay.
Listen carefully.
Your obedience is not the price of God's forgiveness. It is the fruit of a life being transformed by His grace.
And John knew the difference.
Earlier in the same letter, he wrote:
“And he is the propitiation for our sins: and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world.” — 1 John 2:2 (KJV)
The word translated “propitiation” is ἱλασμός (hilasmos).
It describes Christ's atoning sacrifice, through which the problem of human sin before a holy God is decisively addressed.
This is not God pretending evil doesn't matter.
This is not a sentimental pardon that ignores justice.
This is the Father sending His Son to accomplish the redemption we could never accomplish.
John makes that even clearer in the immediate context of our passage:
“Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.” — 1 John 4:10 (KJV)
There it is.
The foundation of Christian assurance.
Not that we loved God perfectly.
But that He loved us first.
Not that our record became spotless through our own effort.
But that Jesus came to deal with our sin.
Not that we rescued ourselves from judgment.
But that the Savior came to rescue sinners.
Imagine standing in a courtroom.
Every accusation against you is true.
Every selfish motive.
Every hidden compromise.
Every cruel word.
Every moment you chose darkness over light.
There is no clever defense.
No excuse strong enough.
No religious accomplishment capable of erasing the evidence.
The Judge is righteous.
The law is holy.
And you know you are guilty.
Then you discover that the One who died and rose again is the very Savior in whom you have placed your trust.
The debt of sin has not been ignored.
Christ has borne it.
The sacrifice has not been left unfinished.
Jesus declared, “It is finished” (John 19:30).
And now the believer stands before God not on the strength of personal innocence, but through the saving work of Jesus Christ.
This courtroom picture is an illustration, but the biblical promise behind it is unmistakable:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1 (KJV)
Read those words again.
No condemnation.
Not reduced condemnation.
Not postponed condemnation.
Not condemnation waiting to return the moment you remember an old failure.
No condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
That promise does not belong to everyone regardless of their relationship with Christ. Scripture calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
But for those who truly belong to Him, the verdict rests upon the sufficiency of their Savior.
And that changes everything.
It means you can stop treating your shame as though it has more authority than the cross.
It means you can confess sin without imagining that confession must persuade an unwilling God to become merciful.
It means you can approach Him honestly because Jesus Christ is your Advocate.
John himself wrote:
“My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.” — 1 John 2:1 (KJV)
Notice both sides.
That ye sin not.
And…
If any man sin, we have an advocate.
John does not give Christians permission to make peace with rebellion.
Neither does he tell a fallen believer that failure automatically means the Savior has abandoned them.
He calls us away from sin while directing our hope toward Christ.
That is the beauty of biblical grace.
It does not excuse the darkness.
It brings us into the light.
It does not tell the adulterer that adultery is harmless.
It calls the sinner to repentance and a transformed life.
It does not tell the dishonest person that lies don't matter.
It calls them to truth.
It does not tell the wounded person that healing means pretending nothing happened.
It brings pain before a Savior who understands suffering.
And it does not tell the struggling Christian to hide until they become worthy of God's presence.
It calls them to confess, repent, trust, and walk in the light.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved to sin. Grace is God's undeserved kindness that brings sinners to Christ and teaches them to live differently.
But there's another misunderstanding we need to confront.
Some Christians hear “perfect love casts out fear” and assume that reverence toward God must disappear.
Yet the Bible repeatedly teaches the fear of the Lord.
Proverbs 9:10 says:
“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.”
The Hebrew expression is:
יִרְאַת יְהוָה
Yir'at YHWH.
The noun יִרְאָה (yir'ah) can describe fear, reverence, or awe, depending on its context.
In Proverbs, the fear of the Lord is the reverent recognition of who God is—His holiness, authority, wisdom, and rightful claim upon our lives.
It is not the same thing as the punishment-centered terror John addresses in 1 John 4.
One kind of fear draws us into humble worship.
The other leaves the guilty conscience expecting condemnation.
One recognizes God's holiness and turns toward Him in reverence.
The other can leave us trembling as though Christ's atonement were insufficient.
And Scripture can speak of both without contradiction.
Hebrews 12:28 calls believers to serve God with reverence and godly fear.
First John 4:18 teaches that mature love casts out the fear associated with punishment.
The love of Christ does not make God less holy. It changes how the redeemed sinner stands before His holiness.
Think about a child who has done something wrong.
There is a difference between a child who respects a loving father's authority and a child who believes every failure means being permanently thrown out of the family.
The first can admit wrongdoing, receive correction, and grow.
The second may hide, lie, and live in terror.
Human parents are imperfect, and this illustration cannot capture everything about God's relationship with His people.
But it helps us understand why assurance and obedience are not enemies.
The believer does not need to choose between loving God and taking sin seriously.
The Gospel gives us reason to do both.
And perhaps nowhere is this more beautifully illustrated than in one of Jesus' most unforgettable stories.
A young man demanded his inheritance.
He left home.
He wasted what he had been given.
And eventually, he found himself hungry, humiliated, and desperate.
The son in Luke 15 had brought disgrace upon himself.
He knew it.
He rehearsed his confession.
He planned to return not as a son expecting privilege, but as someone willing to become a hired servant.
And then Jesus tells us something extraordinary.
“But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.” — Luke 15:20 (KJV)
The father ran.
Before the son could complete his proposed speech about becoming a hired servant, the father was already welcoming him home.
The son still confessed his sin.
His rebellion was not called righteousness.
His wasted years were not celebrated as wisdom.
But the father did not make the son purchase his restoration.
The parable shows the joy of repentance and the extraordinary mercy of God toward returning sinners.
And while the story is not a direct exposition of 1 John 4:18, it reveals the same gracious character of God that John proclaims through Christ.
Now imagine that son returning home…
Only to spend every evening sleeping outside the gate because he could not believe his father had really welcomed him.
Imagine him refusing to sit at the family table.
Imagine him waking each morning convinced that today would be the day his father changed his mind.
How heartbreaking that would be.
And yet something similar happens in the spiritual lives of many believers.
They have heard the Gospel.
They have confessed Christ.
They know the words of forgiveness.
But inwardly, they still live outside the gate.
Still punishing themselves.
Still replaying yesterday.
Still assuming that shame is proof of holiness.
But shame and repentance are not the same thing.
Repentance agrees with God about sin and turns toward Him.
Destructive shame can become so consumed with the self that it forgets to look toward the Savior.
And there is a difference between the Holy Spirit convicting you of sin and the condemning thought that tells you Christ could never receive you.
Conviction calls you into the light.
The Gospel calls you to Christ.
And in Christ, forgiveness is not a reward for pretending to be clean.
It is mercy for sinners who come to Him.
Perhaps you need to hear that tonight.
You do not have to hide the wound from the Physician.
You do not have to disguise the sin from the Savior.
You do not have to manufacture a perfect spiritual performance before you are allowed to seek His mercy.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come trusting not in the strength of your feelings, but in the truth of His Word.
And if you're thinking, “But I still feel afraid,” remember this.
John does not teach that every moment of fear proves someone is not a Christian.
The final statement of 1 John 4:18 says:
“He that feareth is not made perfect in love.”
The language points to love not yet having reached its intended maturity in that person.
It is a call toward deeper assurance, not a simplistic test that labels every anxious believer faithless.
Christian growth is real.
So is struggle.
A believer may know the truth and still need to learn to rest in it more deeply.
The disciples themselves experienced fear.
Paul described pressures and fears in 2 Corinthians 7:5.
And in Gethsemane, Jesus faced profound anguish as He approached the suffering of the cross.
The sinless Son did not lack love because He experienced anguish.
Therefore, we must never use John's words to shame people who experience anxiety, grief, trauma, or emotional distress.
A frightened nervous system is not automatically evidence of spiritual rebellion.
And receiving appropriate support, including professional care when needed, is not a betrayal of faith.
John's focus is specific.
Love brought to maturity gives believers confidence before God's judgment because their hope rests in Jesus Christ.
That confidence is not arrogance.
It is not claiming to know everything about ourselves.
It is not denying that God will judge evil.
It is trusting the One who bore our sins and rose again.
And there is something astonishing about the verse that follows.
“We love him, because he first loved us.” — 1 John 4:19 (KJV)
Not because we finally became impressive.
Not because we collected enough good deeds.
Not because we reached a level of spiritual perfection that forced heaven to notice us.
Because He first loved us.
This is the order of grace.
God's love comes first.
Our response follows.
And that order matters more than many Christians realize.
Because if you reverse it, the entire Christian life becomes a desperate attempt to earn what can only be received through Christ.
You begin treating worship as a transaction.
Prayer becomes a performance.
Giving becomes a payment for divine approval.
Obedience becomes an anxious attempt to prevent rejection.
But when you understand the Gospel, these things begin to change.
You worship because He is worthy.
You pray because He welcomes you through Christ.
You obey because you love the Savior who rescued you.
You give because you want to serve His purposes and care for others.
Not because your money can buy forgiveness.
Not because a ministry can sell you access to God.
Jesus Christ has already paid the price of redemption that no human contribution could ever pay.
And that truth must remain at the center of every Christian ministry, including ours.
At Gospel Warrior, our calling is to keep pointing people back to Jesus Christ through Scripture, repentance, grace, discipleship, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
Because somewhere tonight, a person is reading Christian content while quietly wondering whether God could still receive them.
Somewhere, a husband is hiding a spiritual struggle from his wife.
A mother is carrying guilt from years she cannot recover.
A young believer is exhausted from trying to look stronger than they feel.
A prodigal is afraid to return.
A churchgoer has learned how to smile while living under the crushing weight of condemnation.
And someone who has never truly understood the Gospel is one honest encounter with Scripture away from realizing that Jesus did not come to congratulate the righteous.
He came to save sinners.
We want that message to keep reaching people.
Not merely to create content that receives attention for a few seconds.
But to place biblical truth where wounded hearts, searching minds, and struggling believers can encounter it again and again.
Not because God measures your love by an algorithm.
But because someone in your circle may never tell you how desperately they needed these words.
They might never comment.
They might never message you.
They might simply read, close their phone, open their Bible, and begin praying for the first time in months.
And you may never know.
But the Lord knows.
Not to expose their struggles, but to remind them that the door of repentance and faith in Christ is not closed.
And please, don't leave this conversation without sharing what God is teaching you.
You don't need to reveal private details. You don't need to pretend you have everything figured out.
You can simply be honest.
Your words may help another believer realize they are not alone in the struggle to trust God's promises.
Return to it when the old accusations come back.
Read 1 John 4 again.
Read Romans 8.
Read the Gospel accounts of Christ's death and resurrection.
Let Scripture—not the loudest voice of your emotions—teach you what is true about the Savior.
We want this community to be a place where people encounter biblical truth, receive encouragement, are challenged toward repentance, and keep growing in their understanding of Jesus Christ.
And for those who want to help sustain and expand this work, there is another meaningful way to stand with us.
For some believers, this may be part of their planned monthly giving to Christian ministry.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Without pressure.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share Scripture matters.
Your faithfulness to Christ matters far more than any financial contribution to our ministry.
These are small ways of expressing our appreciation, but the deepest value of your partnership is not a discount or a product.
It is the opportunity to help make Gospel-centered teaching available to more people.
The resources are there to encourage Bible reading, spiritual growth, and a deeper walk with the Lord.
Not to earn God's love.
But, if you choose, to help us tell more people about the love He has already demonstrated in Jesus Christ.
That Christ would be glorified.
That sinners would repent.
That weary believers would find renewed assurance in the Gospel.
That broken lives would be transformed by grace.
Because this is what the message of Jesus does.
It enters the places we would rather keep hidden.
It confronts what we have done.
It exposes the lies we have believed.
And then it points us to the cross, where the seriousness of sin and the greatness of God's love meet.
Perhaps your life has been marked by scandal.
Perhaps you have disappointed people who trusted you.
Perhaps your past contains chapters you wish you could tear out.
Perhaps you have spent years believing that the worst thing you ever did must become the final definition of who you are.
But the Gospel announces something greater than your history.
It announces Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
It announces forgiveness to repentant sinners.
It announces reconciliation with God through the Savior.
It announces a new life that is not built upon pretending the past never happened, but upon the redeeming work of the One who came to save the lost.
This is not cheap grace.
It cost the Son of God His life.
And because He rose again, those who belong to Him have a living hope.
So when John says perfect love casts out fear, hear what he is actually proclaiming.
You do not need to stand before God trusting your ability to erase your past.
You need Jesus Christ.
You do not need to convince yourself that your sins were insignificant.
You need the Savior whose sacrifice is sufficient.
You do not need to become fearless in every circumstance to prove that you belong to Him.
You are called to trust Him, grow in His love, walk in His light, and find assurance in what He has accomplished.
And one day, when the final judgment comes, every false refuge will fall away.
Human reputation will not save us.
Religious performance will not save us.
Money, influence, and popularity will not save us.
Our hope is Christ alone.
So come to Him.
If you have never repented and believed, turn to Him today.
If you are a believer who has wandered, confess your sin and return.
If you are exhausted from trying to earn what Jesus freely gives, remember His finished work.
If you are trembling beneath the weight of condemnation, open the Scriptures and look again at the Savior.
Because the answer to the fear John described is not a stronger version of yourself.
It is a deeper confidence in Jesus Christ.
And perhaps tonight, the most important change in your life will not be that you suddenly feel brave.
Perhaps it will be that, for the first time in a long time, you stop running away from God in shame and begin drawing near to Him through Christ.
Not because you have become worthy.
But because Jesus is worthy.
Not because your story was never broken.
But because His grace is greater than the brokenness of those He redeems.
And when you finally understand that, you may discover something your frightened heart has needed to hear for years:
The cross was not God's invitation for you to spend the rest of your life trying to pay Him back. It was the place where Jesus accomplished the salvation you could never purchase.
The fear kept telling you that your past would have the final word. But for those who belong to Christ, the final word belongs to the Savior who died and rose again.
